citation: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke rt-PA Stroke Study Group. Tissue plasminogen activator for acute ischemic stroke. N Engl J Med. 1995;333(24):1581-1587
one_liner: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke treated within 3 hours, intravenous alteplase improved 3-month disability outcomes across multiple scales (Part 2 global OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2-2.6), with increased symptomatic ICH (6.4% vs 0.6%) but no mortality difference (17% vs 21%, p=0.30).

pico.population: Adults with acute ischaemic stroke, clearly defined time of onset, measurable neurologic deficit on NIHSS, baseline CT without intracranial haemorrhage, treatment start within 3 hours.
pico.intervention: Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% as bolus, remainder infused over 60 minutes. No anticoagulants/antiplatelets for 24 h; blood pressure maintained within prespecified limits.
pico.comparison: Matching placebo, identical bolus/infusion schedule and post-treatment constraints (including 24 h antithrombotic avoidance, BP targets).
pico.outcome: Primary (Part 2): Global test across four 3-month disability measures (Barthel Index 95-100, mRS 0-1, Glasgow Outcome Scale 1, NIHSS 0-1).

background.existing_knowledge: Acute ischaemic stroke was a leading cause of death and long-term disability with limited acute disease-modifying therapies available. Reperfusion with intravenous thrombolysis was biologically plausible but carried a feared trade-off of intracranial haemorrhage and early harm.
background.knowledge_gap: Definitive evidence on whether very-early intravenous alteplase (rt‑PA) could improve neurologic and functional outcomes with an acceptable safety profile was lacking.
background.hypothesis: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke treated within 3 hours, intravenous alteplase improves neurologic recovery at 24 hours (Part 1) and functional outcomes at 3 months (Part 2) compared with placebo.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; stratified by clinical centre and time from onset to start of treatment (0–90 vs 91–180 minutes); two sequential parts with different primary endpoints.
methods.setting: Hospital-based acute stroke care with urgent CT and laboratory evaluation.

inclusion: Acute ischaemic stroke with clearly defined time of onset
Measurable neurologic deficit on the NIH Stroke Scale
exclusion: Stroke or serious head trauma in prior 3 months
GI or urinary tract haemorrhage in prior 21 days
Arterial puncture at noncompressible site in prior 7 days
Systolic BP >185 mmHg or diastolic BP >110 mmHg (including if aggressive lowering required)
Anticoagulant use or heparin in prior 48 hours with elevated aPTT

methods.intervention: Intravenous alteplase (rt‑PA) 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg): 10% as initial bolus, remainder infused over 60 minutes. No anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents for 24 h after treatment; blood pressure maintained within prespecified limits.
methods.comparison: Matching placebo administered using the same bolus/infusion schedule and the same post-treatment constraints (antithrombotic avoidance for 24 h, identical BP targets).
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, treating teams, outcome assessors). CT scans interpreted centrally by a radiologist blinded to clinical information including treatment assignment.
methods.sample_size_power: Part 2 planned 320 patients (160 per group) to detect a 20 percentage point difference with 95% power at 5% significance; actual enrolment 333 (168 alteplase, 165 placebo).
methods.primary_outcome: Part 2: Global test across four 3-month disability measures (Barthel Index 95–100, mRS 0–1, Glasgow Outcome Scale 1, NIHSS 0–1). Part 1: early neurologic improvement (≥4-point NIHSS improvement or complete resolution) at 24 hours.
secondary_outcomes: Individual disability scale endpoints at 3 months (Barthel, mRS, GOS, NIHSS)
methods.follow_up: 3 months (primary); safety CT at 24 h and 7–10 days.

headline_bullets: Alteplase improved 3-month disability across multiple scales (e.g., mRS 0–1: 39% vs 26% in Part 2).
Symptomatic ICH within 36 h was higher with alteplase (6.4% vs 0.6%; P<0.001); 90-day mortality not statistically different (17% vs 21%; P=0.30).
Efficacy present in both time strata (global OR 1.9 for 0–90 and 91–180 min).

outcomes_table.note: Global test across Barthel, mRS, GOS, NIHSS.
Improvement defined as ≥4-point NIHSS improvement or complete resolution.

subgroup_table.subgroup: Onset-to-treatment 0–90 min – Global statistic at 3 months
Onset-to-treatment 91–180 min – Global statistic at 3 months

safety: Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage within 36 hours: 6.4% (alteplase) vs 0.6% (placebo), P<0.001.
All-cause mortality at 90 days: 17% vs 21%, P=0.30 (not significant).
Minor external bleeding within 10 days: 23% vs 3%.
New ischaemic stroke during follow-up: similar rates between groups (Part 1: 8% vs 7%; Part 2: 4% vs 4%).

domains.notes: Permuted-block randomisation (varying block size) stratified by centre and time-to-treatment (0–90 vs 91–180 min). Allocation concealment not detailed, but identical placebo and blinding reduce risk.
Double-blind; central blinded CT interpretation by a radiologist unaware of treatment. Clinical outcome assessors certified and not involved in initial treatment.

Minimal missing primary outcome data: Part 1 missing 1 of 291; Part 2 missing 7 of 1332 measures across 4 patients, handled prespecifically (later measurements or worst-score assignment). ITT analysis maintained.
High dose delivery: Part 1 full dose (±5%) in 90% (alteplase) vs 92% (placebo); Part 2 in 93% vs 93%. Crossover not reported.

Overall similar stroke severity (median NIHSS 14 vs 14 in Part 1; 14 vs 15 in Part 2). Notable imbalances: weight in Part 1 (76 ± 15 kg vs 80 ± 18 kg), age in Part 2 (69 ± 12 vs 66 ± 13 years) – additional covariate adjustment performed when P<0.05.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong given double-blinding, stratified randomisation, high protocol adherence, and minimal missing outcomes, although the two-part structure and modest baseline imbalances warrant attention when interpreting effect sizes.

domains.notes: Typical moderate-severity ischaemic strokes (median NIHSS 14–15) enrolled. Only patients presenting and treatable within 3 hours eligible; minor/rapidly improving strokes, recent bleeding risks, and uncontrolled hypertension excluded.

Findings translate best to systems with rapid prehospital recognition and streamlined in-hospital workflows (urgent CT, stroke expertise, BP control). Limited where onset-to-needle time routinely exceeds 3 hours or imaging/laboratory infrastructure is constrained.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: results are highly applicable to patients meeting the strict early-presenter criteria in stroke-capable systems, but less generalisable to the broader stroke population who present later or fall outside trial eligibility constraints.

strengths: Rigorous randomised double-blind design; multicentre enrolment.
Standardised alteplase dosing with central blinded CT interpretation.
Clinically meaningful 3-month disability outcomes using multiple validated instruments.
Minimal missing outcome data with prespecified handling.
limitations: Two-part design with different primary endpoints complicates overall interpretation.
Modest sample size by modern standards.
Strict eligibility and very-early treatment window limit generalisability.
Increased symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage risk requires careful translation into real-world systems and governance.

critical_appraisal.summary: This trial provides high-quality evidence that alteplase improves functional outcomes when given within 3 hours of acute ischemic stroke, with a manageable increase in symptomatic ICH. Internal validity is strong, though modest baseline imbalances and the two-part design reduce confidence slightly. External validity is limited to early presenters in organized stroke systems.
strengths: Robust double-blind, placebo-controlled design with stratified randomisation
Central blinded CT reading and blinded outcome assessment
Prespecified global disability endpoint that captures a patient-centred benefit
Minimal missing data and ITT analysis
weaknesses: Two-part structure with different primaries; Part 1 acted as a dose-finding phase
Modest sample size (Part 2 n=333) limits power for subgroups and safety estimates
Strict time window (≤3 h) and extensive exclusions reduce generalisability
Baseline imbalances (weight, age) required post-hoc adjustment

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke treated within 3 hours, intravenous alteplase improved the chance of minimal or no disability at 3 months across multiple functional measures, at the cost of increased symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage, without a significant effect on mortality.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial established intravenous alteplase as standard of care for acute ischemic stroke within 3 hours, shifting stroke care to a time-critical emergency model.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with acute ischaemic stroke presenting within 3 hours, without major bleeding contraindications, in systems capable of rapid imaging, laboratory evaluation, and stroke expertise.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Alteplase does not reduce mortality; its benefit is in reducing disability. It does not obviate the need for endovascular therapy in large vessel occlusion.
implementation_caveats: Strict adherence to eligibility criteria and blood pressure control is essential to minimise ICH risk.
Door-to-needle time should be minimised; protocols for rapid assessment and treatment must be in place.
Antiplatelet/anticoagulant avoidance for 24 hours post-thrombolysis is mandatory.

controversies.notes: Accompanying editorial framed thrombolysis as crossing a clinical threshold while emphasising the necessity of system-level readiness and careful patient selection in view of haemorrhagic risk.

Debate focused on whether chance baseline imbalances and the two-part structure could inflate apparent benefit; a formal reanalysis of the NINDS dataset reported that baseline imbalance did not account for the observed treatment effect and supported the trial’s primary conclusions.

Subsequent pooled and individual-patient meta-analytic evidence reinforced a strong time-to-treatment relationship for intravenous alteplase, with greatest net benefit early and attenuation with delay, contextualising the NINDS ‘within 3 hours’ window as the high-yield part of a broader time-dependent effect spectrum.

Implementation studies demonstrated that thrombolysis could be delivered in routine practice with acceptable haemorrhage rates, but also highlighted frequent protocol deviations and the importance of governance, audit, and time-based quality targets for safe scale-up.

Major contemporary guidelines incorporate the NINDS paradigm: intravenous alteplase is recommended for eligible patients treated within 3 hours, with additional selection criteria used for extended windows and special populations in later evidence syntheses.

unresolved_questions: Optimal thrombolysis in extended time windows (3–4.5 hours) and wake-up strokes.
Balancing ICH risk with benefit in milder strokes or patients with extensive early ischaemic changes.
Integration with endovascular therapy in large vessel occlusion.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Alteplase within 3 hours of acute ischaemic stroke improves functional outcomes (disability) at 3 months, with an acceptable increase in symptomatic ICH and no mortality difference.
